When they were done, the pouch came back with the leaf tie folded tighter and a small twist of salt inside. La-la tasted a grain and blinked. "Good sharp," she said. Hakaka tipped the twist into Ya-la’s palm. "Ledger," she said. Ya-la touched the ash floor with two fingers and then her chest. "In us," she said. "Underfoot," the old woman added, because she had to.

Sa-la licked the clay off his thumbs and looked at the line. "Tomorrow?" he asked. Hakaka shook her head. "Next fish, first bite still theirs," she said. Across, as if hearing, the woman lifted the blue knot and tied it to her wrist with the boy’s scrap. The man set his palm to his chest and raised it a little, the smallest thanks.

Before dark, Hakaka retied the signal cord and touched the knot. "Share first bite," she said. La-la touched it. Ya-la touched it. Sa-la touched it. Across the river, three hands did the same. Then the night took the light down, and the line lay quiet between banks like a promise that didn’t need more words.

Mark: forked stake · blue/white strip
Vow: Leave one gap.

Morning ran steady and low. Taro waded to the thigh with a forked pole and felt for hard bottom. "Here," he said. Across, the cliff man stepped out to match him, slow and sure. They pointed with their poles until both tips agreed.

La-la set the first stake. She leaned it a hair upstream. "So the pull makes it truer," she said. Sa-la held the lash. Ya-la kept the coil clean. Hakaka picked two hammer stones, one for each bank, same weight in the hand.

They tied the law to the peg where anyone could grab it: one knot--set; two knots--brace; red bead--stop. Ya-la slotted a white scrap beside the blue on the signal strip. "Blue means river. White means stone. Both means both hands," she said. The boy across copied, tongue out, careful.

They drove the first pair together. La-la’s stone spoke three times; across, the cliff man answered three. The stakes sat. The line between them took a soft curve and stopped arguing. "Next," Hakaka said.

A shallow throat took shape: stakes in a V that pointed downstream toward an open mouth where a basket would live. Taro split reeds with a rib sliver and twisted fast. Sa-la tried his speed and dropped a lash. La-la didn’t look at him. "Slow wins," she said. He slowed. The lash held.

The woman across showed a faster tie--half-knot, twist, tuck. She did it without pride. Sa-la copied. His first tuck slipped; his second did not. He did not look up for praise. The dog watched a dragonfly and pretended not to care.

They seated the basket. Reed throat, tight weave, mouth tied to the inside stakes with two loops that would give a little and no more. La-la tested it with her fist and then with a tug. "Good," she said. "It won’t lie."

First test: a silver body nosed the V, felt the basket mouth, and went in because it didn’t know better. The throat narrowed behind it. Taro moved to lift; Hakaka shook her head once. "Let it calm," she said. They waited till the fish stopped writing panic. Then La-la lifted the basket just enough for water to keep speaking around it.

Ya-la slid her hand in and took the small one, not the largest. She turned and showed the others: alive, quick. She set it free through the vow gap. Across, the boy grinned, full teeth. The cliff man gave one slow nod. The old woman coughed and said, "Good manners," like she was tired of being right.
They emptied the basket proper. Three fat fish went to shore--one laid on a cool stone for trade, two for stew. Ya-la tied a blue strip to the trade one. Sa-la reset the throat, hands steady now.
Wind freshened. Floats ticked the line wrong. Hakaka pointed. "Wider by one hand." La-la slid them out. The ticking stopped.

Near dusk they walked the weir once, each stake with a palm on it, checking for wobble and lies. A soft place sucked at La-la’s heel. "Mark it," she said. Taro cut a notch in the nearest stake, waist-high, so a tired body would see it even in bad light.

Before they went, Hakaka touched the vow stone. "Still a gap," she said. La-la touched it too. Ya-la did. Sa-la did. Across the river, four hands did the same. Then the light went thin, and the weir hummed its small, work sound, and both banks went to make fire.

Mark: peg pair · blue notch
Vow: Agree before pull.

Morning gave them a steady seam. Taro set a peg high on their bank where the line ran true. Across, the cliff man answered with a peg opposite, slow and exact. They didn’t tie a rope across; they let the water keep its spine.

La-la shaved thin floats from reed and slid them on the pouch line like beads, one hand apart. "Shows where it rides," she said. Sa-la counted the gaps with his thumb. "Don’t lose the count," La-la said, not unkind.

Ya-la cut a short strip and marked one end with a single blue notch. "Throw," she said, tapping the notch. She tied two notches on another. "Wait." She rubbed a red bead with ash and set it beside both. "Danger." She did it slow so her hands would remember. Hakaka watched and said nothing.

They sent the first pouch light--two roots, a sliver of smoked fat, the "throw" strip. It rode, dipped, chose the inside curve, and came to the woman. The woman held up her own strip: two notches. She didn’t take the pouch. Ya-la lifted her hand, palm down. Wait. The boy pointed at a back-eddy farther down. A branch rolled in it like a lazy animal.

La-la nodded. "If we pull now it snags." She pinched the line, felt the seam talking. "It’ll clear in three breaths." They breathed with it. On the third breath the branch slipped its sulk and went on. The woman dropped her strip, lifted one notch, once. Throw. Sa-la smiled with his mouth closed. La-la eased the line. The woman took the pouch then, as agreed. She put in three small fish, bright still, and a thumb of salt in leaf, tight-wrapped. She sent it back with the "wait" strip and the red bead on top, to say both sides knew why.

They tested the "pull" itself. Hakaka tied a dull stone in another pouch and slid it out until it kissed the seam’s shoulder and thought about sticking. She looked up. The woman had already set one foot back and braced. Ya-la raised two fingers, closed them, opened--together. Both sides leaned, not hard, just enough to speak to the snag. The pouch shivered loose and came on. No one slipped. The old woman’s mouth twitched; she pretended it was the smoke.

They wrote the rule plain. La-la knotted a short cord: one knot near the end, throw; two knots apart, wait; two knots pinched together, pull together. Ya-la added the red bead on a loop that slid. She hung it by their peg where hands would find it in the dark. Across, the woman did the same with different cord and same law. The boy touched both and laughed once, small.

Wind turned and lied for a while. The floats began to chatter, bumping the line wrong. Sa-la reached to snatch the near float; Hakaka caught his wrist. "Watch first." The chatter settled into a new count: slower, farther apart. "Now," Hakaka said. La-la slid the floats wider by one hand. The line went quiet again. Sa-la grinned at the simple fix and didn’t say a word. He moved the spare floats to match and checked the count without being told. The dog lay on his feet and agreed by staying.

Near noon a shadow came--otter or something like it--sleek and certain. It nosed the pouch, curious and rude. Across the water the boy hissed; Sa-la nearly hissed back. Ya-la lifted the red bead high and then put it down on the bank beside her knee: danger, but not for pulling. They all stilled. The animal lost interest and wrote nothing, slid on. The old woman coughed once and called it stupid under her breath like a blessing.

They closed the day with one last exchange: Ya-la sent their "wait" strip back across on purpose. The woman tied their two-notch to her own peg with a simple knot, no making it pretty. The cliff man looked at both pegs and gave one short nod. Taro carved a notch across the tops of both their pegs, same angle, so even the moon would read it.

Hakaka stood a moment with her palm on their peg, feeling the river think. "Bridge without weight," she said. La-la checked the floats one more time. Ya-la covered the salt leaf so no one salted their tongue for want of sense. Sa-la tied the spare cord to the peg base and tugged it once, firm and honest.

At dusk the far camp hung their two-knot cord where wet light could find it. Ya-la lifted theirs to match. Both sides let the pegs keep watch. The wind shifted again and tried to confuse the floats. The floats told the truth anyway.

Mark: blue twist · ash water
Vow: Color without waste; signal without lies.
They made lye first. Ya-la poured warm water through last night’s ash into a clay cup until it felt slick between two fingers. "Not strong," she said. "Just enough to wake it."

Hakaka unrolled the blue twist on a flat stone. It bled a pale green that wanted to hide. Sa-la leaned in with the cup. "Slow," La-la told him, and moved his hand a thumb’s width. Ya-la dripped lye a drop at a time. The wet turned the green darker, not blue yet. "Air," Hakaka said. They waited and watched it breathe into color. It did. The old woman nodded once like a debt paid on time.

They needed a thread that would keep it. Taro split a dry reed and teased out the strong skin. Sa-la twisted two skins together, polite this time. Ya-la dipped the cord, wrung it with her palm, lifted it to the air. It came up green, then shifted as the wind thought about it. Blue found it like river light. Sa-la grinned and looked down fast so it wouldn’t feel chased.

Across the bend, the far people watched. The scar-mouth woman stood with her hands behind her back so her shoulders wouldn’t talk. The boy shaded his eyes. The cliff man set a small pot near their hump and didn’t touch it again.

La-la prepped three more cords. "Test," she said. One they dipped and lifted. One they dipped, dried, dipped again. One they rubbed with fat first. The fat one sulked and took nothing. "Not for coats," La-la said. "Skin before color and color goes hungry." Sa-la held the failed cord anyway because it felt good.

They tried cloth. Ya-la cut a thin strip from the robe’s spare hem and tied it to a peg, not the robe itself. "We don’t learn on what keeps us," Hakaka said. Ya-la dipped the strip, wrung, lifted. The blue climbed from the edges in. "Two breaths," Ya-la said to herself, and counted them out. She set the strip in shade. "Shade holds it," she said. "Sun steals quick." La-la moved the strip without being asked when the sun reached for it.

The old woman sucked the edge of her tooth and pointed at the ash cup. "Keep it covered," she said. "Air eats everything." Sa-la set a shard over it like a lid and put a small stone on top so his hand would remember.

They made signs. Hakaka laid a reed on the ground and tied two blue knots near one end. "With," she said, touching both knots. She tied one knot in the middle. "Again." Ya-la added a fish scale beside the middle knot. "River." La-la frowned, then nodded. "Not pretty. True." Sa-la tried to tie the middle knot blind, eyes closed; he got it after three tries. He left the wrong knots on the ground and did not kick them.

They sent a message. In the reed pouch they put the blue-knotted strip, two pebbles, a fish scale, a small pinch of oven paste wrapped in leaf. Hakaka looked at the river, then at Sa-la. "Flat and low," she said. He threw flat and low. The pouch rode a seam like it knew the way home better than either side.

The woman took it. She opened the leaf, tasted with the tip of her tongue like a cat that still had pride. She touched the blue knots and looked at their wrists. She spoke to the boy without moving her mouth. He ran and came back with a cord they’d dyed wrong--too long in the sun; it had gone dull. She did not throw it away. She tied it into the pouch with a hook wire and a small clay bead the color of dry blood. She added three pebbles, not two. She sent it back.

La-la poured the pebbles into her palm and sorted their meanings with her face. "Three?" Sa-la said. Ya-la tapped the bead. "Not food," she said. She put it to her nose. It smelled like river clay cooked too hot. She rubbed it on her wrist. It left a fat mark that didn’t move. "Mark," she said. She drew a thin blue line across the red. "Ours with theirs," Hakaka said. The old woman held out her hand. Ya-la marked her knuckle. The old woman didn’t look at it. "Don’t waste it," she said.

They made a thing to show and not shout. La-la shaved a flat of reed and bent it into a small circle, tied with a plain cord. Ya-la wove the blue strip through it: over, under, over, under, leaving the ends to flutter. "Wind door," La-la said, and hung it near the shelter mouth so you could read it from the river. Hakaka put one blue dot above the circle in ash and wiped it away, then put it again. "Tomorrow," she said. "No hiding."

Sa-la wanted his own bit. He asked with his eyes. Ya-la gave him the dull-blue strip. "Practice," she said. He tied three knots fast and wrong, then slower and right. He wore it around his wrist and did not show it to the far boy. The dog came and sniffed the strip. Sa-la let it and didn’t pretend to kick.

Work kept moving. They rinsed the lye cup, saved the blue water in a small pot, and tied a grass slip around its neck so no one drank it in the dark. Taro drove a thin peg at the bank where the seam ran truest. "Throw from here," he said to his own feet. The old woman tucked the green powder tight and forgot to cough for a little while.

Near dusk the far camp answered. They lifted a strip the color of river skin at evening--grey that wanted blue and didn’t dare. It hung from a stick planted in the wet. The woman tapped her chest once and then held up three fingers, dropped one, held two. Ya-la answered with two fingers and a flat hand--same, stay. The cliff man stood behind her like he was part of the bank. The boy copied Sa-la’s wrist strip knot without the strip and laughed once, quiet.

Night pulled in the edges. Hakaka tied the blue strip high on the shelter post. La-la moved the wind door a hand toward leeward so it wouldn’t lift in the wrong breath and lie. Ya-la set the lye cup under a pot so children and Sa-la’s hands wouldn’t find it first. Taro made a notch in the bank peg so he could find it blind. The old woman turned her marked knuckle toward the fire when she fell asleep.

"Story?" Sa-la asked. "Small," Hakaka said. "We found a color. We didn’t chase it. It stayed." She tucked the shard over the blue pot’s mouth and put a pebble on it with two fingers. "Tomorrow," she said, and left the pebble there to say it twice.

Mark: ring of stone · small draw
Vow: Wait until the wait turns sweet.
Morning had a bite. Breath showed. Hakaka chose a flat patch above the flood line and paced a circle with her heel. "Here," she said. "Wind comes from there. Slope pulls that way."

La-la scored the circle with a stick. "Two hands wide beyond the biggest thing we’ll cook," she said. Taro measured with his palm. Sa-la brought armfuls of dry grass and the flattest stones. Ya-la filled the water jug and set it in shade. The old woman sat where the sun would get her knees and kept her cough in a tight fist.

They dug shallow first: a bowl of earth as deep as La-la’s wrist. Taro cut a small draw trench from the rim to the downslope--a mouth for air, not greedy. "Heat likes tight," La-la said. She lined the bowl with stones that didn’t ring when tapped; ringers crack. Hakaka thumbed clay into the seams. "No runaway breath."
Sa-la started the first fire in the naked pit, twigs, dry grass, a few thicker sticks. He watched the smoke choose the draw trench. "Good," Hakaka said. "Let the stones learn warm."

They built the dome while the stones drank heat. Ya-la mixed mud with chopped straw and the smallest reeds, kneading until it held a shape when she squeezed it. La-la made a ring of field stones around the pit and bridged them with flat pieces, leaving a hole at the top you could cover with your palm. "It needs a lid that obeys," she said. Taro fetched a broken pot shard that fit like it had been waiting.

Sa-la reached to slap on mud too thick. La-la caught his wrist. "Thin skins first," she said. "Thick falls." He nodded, started again. Thin coat, then another after it quit shining. They smoothed with wet hands until the dome looked like a sleeping animal. Hakaka pressed a small coin of clay over the draw mouth’s rim to remember the wind.

Across the river the far people watched from their bend. The scar-mouthed woman crossed her arms. The boy pointed once; the cliff-shouldered man looked at the sky like it owed him something. Ya-la lifted a hand without waving. "After," she murmured.

The first fire went to coals. Hakaka raked them to the edges so the belly stayed hot and the mud skin didn’t cry. Little cracks spoke. Ya-la smeared them shut. "Quiet," she told the clay. The dome steamed in places you could see. La-la moved her palm near the little top hole and felt the speed the heat wanted. "Cover," she said. Taro set the shard in place. The sound inside changed, low and pleased.

They fed the oven again--small sticks, then thicker, never forcing. Sa-la bent to blow too eager and got a mouthful of ash. He coughed, spat dark, and grinned without pride. "Slow mouth," Ya-la said. He nodded, eyes watering.

Hakaka pulled the heat when the dome turned from wet-dark to dry-pale. They scraped coals into a trench and sealed the draw with a plug of wet grass and clay. The belly of the oven held breath. "Now we wait," Hakaka said.

Waiting had work. La-la sliced roots thin and dusted them with salt. Ya-la worked a paste of ground seeds and water with the little pestle, pushing and folding until it listened. Taro pounded a flat of clay into a tray and dried it by the fire that wasn’t the oven’s fire. Sa-la checked the rim seam three times, because he didn’t trust himself not to bump it. He didn’t bump it.
The old woman watched all this like a judge with a full book. "If it falls," she said, "we eat smoke." "We won’t," La-la answered, not looking up.

They opened the shard lid with cloth around fingers. Heat kissed the air and tried to run. Hakaka let it, just a little. "Feed," she said. The tray went in with the seeds paste spread hand-thick and the root slices on a flat stone beside it. Shard back. "Now we wait right," Hakaka said.

Waiting right meant not peeking. It meant ears and nose instead of eyes. At first they smelled mud and yesterday. Then the smell shifted. Sa-la’s shoulders lowered. "Sweet," he said, surprised. The old woman’s mouth tilted. "Not yet," she warned.

Across the water, a thin shout skimmed the surface. The scar-mouthed woman cupped her hands and sent a sound like two pebbles struck and a long breath. Ya-la lifted a strip of blue and let it hang from her wrist. "Not yet," she echoed, pointing at the dome and the sky in one small line. The boy across laughed without a sound anyone could hear.

A crack webbed the dome near the top hole, the kind that means "enough" not "broken." La-la touched it and felt the heat say yes. "Open," she said. Hakaka took the shard. The smell rose like a soft hand. They pulled the tray and the root stone with sticks. The paste had browned at the edges and blistered where the bubble wanted to be a mouth. The roots had gone from stubborn to willing.

Sa-la reached. La-la’s look stopped him closer than a hand could. "Air first," she said. They waited until the skin quit spitting and the color deepened one shade. Hakaka broke a corner. Steam spoke in a language everyone knew. She gave the old woman the first bite. "About time," the old woman said after chewing it until it quit arguing.

They ate without talking, because hot food has its own conversation. The paste was nut-sweet, a little smoke, a little ash from the edge. The roots were tender with a clean bite. Ya-la wiped her thumb over the tray to chase the last oil and didn’t lick it until she saw Sa-la watching. He smirked and then didn’t.

A dog came, thin and curious. Taro had a stone in his sling before the thought finished. He let it thrum once without release. The dog read the music and kept distance. Ya-la threw a peel that wasn’t food far away and the dog went to re-learn disappointment.

Across the river, smoke rose from a little hump near the far camp. The woman had copied the dome wrong at first--too thick, too hungry a draw. The cliff man knocked the side and the top slid an inch. He didn’t swear. He pressed it back and sealed it with mud. The boy watched, face lit like first fire. Ya-la lifted the shard in her hand and made a circle with two fingers: thin skins. The woman snorted, the sound carrying just enough to be a joke between banks.

When the oven cooled enough to touch, Hakaka tapped the skin here and there. "Lives," she said. She showed Sa-la where to smear the little mouth with clay when the wind forgot itself. She showed Taro how to clear the throat without stealing its shape. La-la made a small wad of grass to keep the shard from ringing and set it beside the hole like a lid’s pillow. Ya-la took a piece of charcoal and drew a round with a small mouth and a smaller mouth on the ash floor near the oven: dome, draw, breathe. Two dots at the rim meant "thin skins." She wiped it clean with her palm and pressed the soot into the floor with the heel of her hand.

They kept a little of the paste for the far side and wrapped it in a leaf that didn’t leak. Hakaka set it in the reed pouch with two pebbles and a fish scale--"with" and "again" and "river" in their new grammar--and handed it to Sa-la. "Easy," she said. He didn’t run. He set the throw flat and low and watched the line, not his own hands.

The pouch drifted to the far bank. The boy stepped and then remembered to wait. The woman lifted the leaf, broke a corner, put it on her tongue. She didn’t change her face. She set another piece in the boy’s hand. The cliff man smelled and gave nothing away. The woman put a flat pinch of ground leaf into the pouch, green and sharp, and a twist of something blue that bled into the leaf like river under ice. She tied the loop better than Sa-la had tied it and sent it back with one small push.

Ya-la untied the blue twist and her fingers came away faintly colored. "Not for eating," she said, smiling with her eyes. The green powder bit the nose and opened the head behind the eyes. The old woman sniffed it and stopped coughing for the space of eight breaths. She handed it back without comment. "Trade," Hakaka said, and no one argued.

They sealed the oven mouth with a clay coin and a flat stone. "Not tight," La-la said. "Let night walk through." Taro set a small line of pebbles beside the dome to show the wind’s road for morning. Sa-la pressed his thumb into the dome’s side once, a soft, private mark, and then rubbed it out with the heel of his hand.

As the light leaned away, the far dome gave a small pop and kept itself. The boy clapped once and the woman pretended not to have heard. The cliff man looked at the river and nodded like it had finally said something sensible.

They cleaned what needed it and left what would teach them tomorrow. Ya-la hung the shard on a peg with a loop of reed. Hakaka moved the water jug into shadow again because it was a habit that saved thinking later. La-la checked the draw mouth one last time and pushed a finger-width of grass into the gap. "Sleep," she told the oven, like you tell a child who listens.

"Story?" Sa-la asked. The old woman lay back and stared at the small blue left on Ya-la’s thumb. "Smallest," she said. Hakaka sat and let her hands warm on her knees. "We were hungry," she said. "We learned slow. We waited right. It fed us." She stopped. That was enough.

Night came. The dome kept a little hum you could only hear if you put your ear against it and forgot pride. Taro took first watch without being told. The dog circled and lay down where it could smell both camps and dream fair.
In the morning, the dome was just dirt that knew a new trick. The ash drawing was gone. The waiting stayed.

Mark: stone V · leader gap
Vow: Let it tire.

The river ran a little lower after three dry days. Stones showed their backs like slow fish. Hakaka stood where the water split around a knee of rock and tapped it with a stick. "Here," she said. "It already chooses."

La-la rolled her sleeves and stepped in to ankle depth. The cold climbed her shins like it meant to live there. "Line the push," she said, and set the first stone where the current helped hold it. Taro brought more, testing each against his thigh so it wouldn’t wobble. He laid them with the flattest face into the flow, tight, no gaps that could argue.

They built a V with its open mouth downstream, the point aimed toward the knee of rock. Hakaka worked at the point with her hands, slow and exact, rubbing mud into the seams like law. "If the point is greedy," she said, "the river will punish it." Ya-la held the basket on her hip and watched how the eddies braided. She folded that into memory where she kept people and weather.
The old woman sat on the bank with the blanket high and her feet bare to the sun. "Catch a fat one," she said, like a queen. Sa-la grinned at her and then kept his face straight when La-la glanced.

They left a narrow path of stones leading into the V, a thin throat that said come this way without shouting. Past the throat, La-la set a low gate of willow stakes and twine. Not tight. Honest. "Don’t scare them," she said. "It’s work, not a fight." Sa-la wove a loose lattice with reed. His first bands crossed wrong and made a proud X that would snag everything. La-la pressed a finger to it. "This is where it will fail." He cut and threaded again. It learned to bend.

Across the water, the far people watched from the bend where sand made a small beach. The woman with the thin scar stood with her hands in her belt. The boy held the blue scrap, quiet this time. The cliff-shouldered man was a tree. Ya-la lifted her chin to them. She did not wave. Work first.

When the V reached mid-calf depth and the point held without complaint, they guided a branch into the throat and let the river push against it. The branch rubbed the stones and spoke in small, wet sounds. "Hear it?" Hakaka asked. Sa-la tilted his head. "It’s telling on the gaps." He moved a stone and the sound eased.

By noon, the weir took shape: two arms gathering water into the throat, a pocket behind the gate where tired fish might think they had a choice. La-la placed three stones near the mouth of the pocket, not in a row, not neat. "They like to hide behind trouble," she said. Taro laughed once under his breath. Ya-la caught it and kept it as a bright thing for later.
They ate cold tuber and a thin strip of meat on the bank. The old woman didn’t ask; Ya-la put a slice on a tile and slid it to her toe. "Too salty," the old woman said, eating.

When they stood again, the river had changed its mind in small ways. The left arm pushed harder, the right grew polite. "Shift," Hakaka said. She and La-la moved six stones as if they were one. The throat narrowed a thumb. Sa-la lifted a rock too big for him and made it look easy until it wasn’t. He grunted, set it, and then sat with the water running cold over his knees. "I will like this later," he announced. Ya-la smiled at the top of her mouth.

They set the basket downstream of the pocket, tied to a willow with a line that had already proved it knew how to return. Hakaka rubbed a little clay into the basket’s mouth so it would receive without bruising. "Soft," she said. "Let them give up without shame."

The first silver backs nosed the arms of the V while the sun leaned west. They came like thoughts--one, then none, then three at once. They tried the throat, felt the narrowing, and pushed harder because pushing is what a body knows. The weir didn’t stop them; it suggested.

A flash slapped the gate and slid along it. The lattice wavered and held. The fish turned and found the pocket and stayed because the pocket told a small lie about safety. Sa-la’s hands tightened on the line. Hakaka touched his wrist. "Wait until the wait turns sweet," she said. He breathed out. He held.

The basket rocked and took a third, smaller fish as if it had decided to help. Sa-la whooped, swallowed it, and looked at Hakaka. She let a corner of her mouth go. "Now," she said. He pulled the basket in and set it where the water could still talk but not argue. He touched the gills with a wet hand to honor the air it used not to breathe.

"Leave one," Hakaka said. "Always one." Sa-la looked at the pocket and looked at her. La-la answered for him. "Or the river keeps its own tax with interest." Sa-la nodded, this time because he understood and not to prove he could.

A dog came from upstream, ribs telling its own story. It skulked near the bank and thought about the basket. Taro stood, put a stone in his sling, and let the sling remind him, once around, twice, release--stone kissed the water hard in front of the dog’s nose. The dog decided it had urgent business elsewhere. The old woman grunted approval like a small drum with a cloth over it.

When the light went to copper, they eased the lattice open and let the pocket empty. Three fish slid out and went where the river always goes. Sa-la watched the last one and made himself not reach. He watched it flick and vanish into the dark line. "Go tell," he said, not loud. Ya-la heard and kept that too.

They carried the basket up to the flat stones. Hakaka chose the two larger fish for eating and one small one for tomorrow’s promise--guts buried near the reed bed, not underfoot. "Where we want more," she said. La-la cleaned fast and neat. Sa-la fetched water and didn’t spill even once. Taro cut thin, true slices with the sharp bone he had made to pay a debt and kept to honor it. The old woman held the salt horn and watched like a priest.

Across the river, the far people built their own V of stones a little wider, a little wrong at the point. Ya-la pointed with her chin, once. La-la shook her head no--work here. Hakaka made no sign. The woman across looked at their hands and changed one stone. The point softened. She did not look up. "Friends after," Ya-la said again, this time audible. No one argued.

When the bones showed clean, Ya-la wrapped them in a leaf and hung them on a branch. "High," Hakaka said. "Dogs have lessons too." Sa-la stood in the shallows and rubbed the slime from his forearms with sand. He looked at the weir in the last light. "We made a trap that respects," he said. La-la snorted soft. "We made a suggestion the river agreed with," she corrected. Hakaka put a hand on both their shoulders. "If it keeps working, it’s a law," she said. "If not, it was a good day."
The old woman shifted to her side and tucked her cold feet under the blanket made of old rope-ends and mistakes. "Tomorrow," she said. "Do it again. Better." Her voice didn’t ask.

Night put its hand on the river and pressed. The knee of rock did its old work without praise. The basket dripped once, then stopped. Hakaka listened until she heard only the sounds that meant rest. "Watch," she said, and Taro touched his chest because it was his turn and he was ready.

Mark: palm-stripe in ash · pebble tally
Vow: Remember without weight.
Morning, they swept the floor clean of last night. Hakaka drew a wide stripe of ash with her palm and blew once to settle it. "Ledger," she said. "Only today."
"Rules first," Hakaka said. La-la spoke them while she pinched the ash flat:

-- Write what happened, not what should have.
-- One mark per work. No fat.
-- Pebbles for numbers larger than hands.
-- At dusk, we read. At dawn, we sweep.
-- Memory goes in backs and feet.

Across the stripe, Hakaka set DEBT / GIFT. She put down a meat-scrap’s shadow with ash for what came from the far bar last night, then a small ring for the clay plug they sent back. "Balance with food or work," she said. "Not with talk."

Midday, the ledger got crowded. The ash grew lumpy; marks blurred where ankles stepped. La-la used a reed tip to sharpen the lines. "Thin tells longer," she said. Ya-la marked FEVER with a single wavy stroke and then HONEY with two dots. The old woman watched and did not argue.

At WATCH, Hakaka wrote names in a column, each with a short tail in the direction they should face. Sa-la reached to put himself on first. Hakaka laid a finger on his wrist. "Second," she said. "You learn better when the edge is near but not yours." He nodded, which meant not yet angry.

A gust pushed at the door. The stripe shivered. Taro slid a flat stone across the threshold to keep footprints off the lower edge. "Stone remembers rules too," he said under breath. The old woman heard. "Stone forgets when dropped," she said. He grinned and didn’t drop it.

Afternoon brought the KILL / SPARE row--La-la’s snares had laughed and let go again. She marked a tuft of hair with three short scratches and tied a real tuft to the robe so the lesson would tug. "Ledger has a hand," Sa-la said, touching the pull. "Use both," Hakaka said.

Across the river, smoke curled different. Ya-la rubbed a shard of clay with charcoal and drew our stripe on it, then a small circle and two pebbles. She sent it by pouch. It came back with a notch cut on the shard’s edge and a line burned with a hot stick. Taro held it up. "Edge means count," he guessed. Ya-la set the shard on the ledger, cut our own notch with a flake, and made a matching burn. "Bridge," Hakaka said. The old woman clicked her tongue, which meant good.

Before dusk, Sa-la palmed two pebbles from WOOD and set them under FIRE. La-la saw. She didn’t speak. She moved the cup. Sa-la’s knee found it. He caught the cup and the look from Hakaka in the same breath. He put the pebbles back. "Write the work your hands remember," Hakaka said. "Or your knee will."

Ya-la read the marks like steps: "Water four. Rope two. Net one new. Wood three. Fire kept, once wrong then right. Fever watched. Honey paid. Gift and debt level." She glanced to Hakaka. "Almost," Hakaka said, tapping the meat-shadow. She added a small ash line for the bite the old woman hadn’t taken. "Truth is the whole mouth."

They set TOMORROW with three empty headings: CLAY, LINE, WATCH. Ya-la put a single ghost-mark under CLAY--not a promise, only a wish. She blew it away with two soft puffs. "Wish belongs in the chest," she said. "Not the floor." The old woman hummed, which meant finally.

Hakaka handed Sa-la a fresh twig. "Sweep." He hesitated. "We’ll forget," he said. "No," Hakaka said. "We will carry." She pointed at his palm, at La-la’s shoulders, at the tug on the robe, at Taro’s flat stone, at Ya-la’s shard with the notch. "Many ledgers."

Before sleep, Ya-la took one black-ended counting stick and burned its other end clean. She set it by the door with the others, black to one side, clean to the other, the way she’d said: hungry/ fed, storm / clear, lost / found. Taro touched the row with two fingers. "How many we didn’t starve," he said. "Today: one more," La-la said.

Mark: clay dome · leaf seal · draw-hole
Vow: Heat once, feed many.
They picked a place out of wind, on hard ground that didn’t drink. Hakaka drew a circle with a stick. "Belly-sized," she said. "Not house-sized."

La-la hauled clay from the bank and stamped it with her heels until it went from slick to willing. Taro pounded dry grass and crushed shell into it for temper. Ya-la carried water; Sa-la carried questions.

"Sand first," Hakaka said. They heaped damp sand into a round back, the way you build a sleeping dog. "Door here." She cut a mouth as wide as her hand and two fingers. "And a small hole at the crown so smoke can tell us its color," the old woman added, settling on a rock.

They laid clay over the sand with hands like paddles--flat, not poking. First a thin skin. Then another. Sa-la smacked a lump high and proud; the clay sagged. "Thin and even," La-la said, smoothing it back down. "Thick breaks."
Cracks showed at the mouth when it started to dry; Ya-la stroked them with wet fingers until they closed. Taro pressed a flat stone at the threshold so the door wouldn’t chew itself.

They left it to stiffen while they cut arm-length sticks. "Small fire first," Hakaka said. "Oven has to learn heat like a child learns walking." Sa-la fed it too fast and the dome hissed. A hairline opened. He flushed, pulled wood back, and breathed until the smoke darkened then cleared. The crack waited, no bigger.
All afternoon they nursed it--stick, ember, wait. The dome changed voice: from damp thud to a clean, hollow knock when La-la tapped it with a twig. "It’s listening," she said.
Evening came cold. They burned the inside bright, then raked the coals out into a shallow trench for tea. The dome held a red glow that was more memory than fire. "Now the roots," Hakaka said.

Ya-la rubbed tubers with a little salt and ash. Taro wrapped them in leaves and damp clay flats as thin as bark. Sa-la slid them in with a forked stick. The old woman pinched the door with a double fold of wet grass and slapped a clay tile against it. "Seal soft," she said. "Hard seals leak."

They sat on their heels and listened to the oven talk--little ticks as the clay settled, a sigh now and then from the door. Sa-la pressed his ear to the dome. "It’s breathing." Hakaka nudged him back. "So are you. Wait."

The smell rose slow, from raw soil to sweet root. When Ya-la said, "There," they pulled the door and rolled the bundles out. The clay shells cracked under thumb; steam lifted. They passed pieces, blew on fingers, burned lips, grinned anyway. The old woman chewed and gave one single nod that meant three things.
They wrote the rule in ash on the ground, where knees had already polished it:

-- Form with sand; skin with thin clay.
-- Temper the clay or it sulks.
-- Small fire teaches; big fire tests.
-- Knock for hollow; watch for hairlines.
-- Rake coals; load fast; seal soft.
-- Wait until the wait turns sweet.
-- Heat once, feed many.
They wiped the line. The rule stayed in their hands.

After, they slid the coals back in for one more bake--flat cakes of pounded seed, the kind you eat with two fingers and a thanks. Hakaka left the door propped with a sliver so smoke would find the crown hole and not their eyes. Sa-la reached to close it; she shook her head. "Let it breathe."

Across the river, the scar-mouthed woman lifted her chin at the new glow. Ya-la held up a flat cake, broke it, set half in the reed pouch, and sent it across. It came back with a small clay plug, shaped neat, just the size of their draw-hole. La-la set it in place and smiled with only one side of her mouth.

Night cooled and the dome held on. They lay near it for the warm and for what it promised: mornings with work that didn’t bite as hard. Sa-la pressed his palm to the clay and learned the feel of enough. The oven forgot nothing. Neither did they.

Mark: forked stakes · brush fence · basket gate
Vow: Take plenty; leave one path.
They walked until the river ran straight and shallow, the bottom clean as a palm. Hakaka paced it with her heel. "Here," she said. "Push with the river, not against."

La-la cut stakes from willow and split their bottoms. Taro carried them to the bar, two at a time, shoulders set. Sa-la wanted the longest; Hakaka handed him the short ones. "You’ll place more and learn faster," she said. He didn’t argue.

They drove the stakes slanted downstream so the push would seat them. La-la’s stone mallet spoke a steady beat. Ya-la brought brush--flex and tangle--and wove it belly-high between stakes. The fence bent and hummed. Good.

They shaped the fence into a wide V pointing with the current. At the narrow end they set a basket with its mouth upstream and a flat stone to keep it from wandering. "Gate here," Hakaka said, tapping a gap a hand-span wide beside the basket. Sa-la reached to close it. Hakaka caught his wrist. "Leave a lane," she said. "River pays us when we pay it back."

First light brought shadows with fins. The fence nudged them toward the mouth. Some slid past the gate and were gone. Sa-la’s jaw went tight. "Wait," La-la said. "Full fences break; patient ones fill."

The first try failed small: a push of water rolled the basket and it sulked sideways, empty. Taro saw it first. He set a second stone on the far side and twisted the basket’s mouth to face truer. Ya-la tied two reeds across the throat to take the first kick of water, not the basket ribs. The mouth held its shape.

By noon the basket knocked once, soft. Ya-la lifted it with Hakaka. Silver flashed--two fish, fat enough for stew and a gift across. They bled them quick and clean. Sa-la grinned, then checked the gate with his thumb. It was still open. He let his grin live.

They worked the line all day: brush tighter where water lied, higher where it climbed. La-la’s hands were striped red; she rubbed silt on the sting and kept weaving. Taro learned the mallet’s rhythm and matched it without showing off. The old woman sat where wind met shade. "Good ear," she said to the fence. No one asked if she meant the wood or the ones who built it.

Across the water the scar-mouth woman watched from her stones. Hakaka lifted the basket and tipped two fish to the current. One slid the gate and was gone. The other rode the flow to their bar. The cliff-man’s gaze moved, slow as a log in flood. He raised a hand, palm out. Fair.

Near dusk a bigger push came--backs cutting the run like knife tips. The basket thunked harder than before, tried to climb free. Sa-la leaped; La-la’s hand thumped his chest. "Not when it’s loud," she said. They waited a breath. The push eased. They lifted together. Four fish. Enough.

They shared the first two, hung two to smoke, and set bones to boil. Ya-la took a small one across in the reed pouch with a blue strip tied near the loop. The woman on the far bar sent back a coil of thin cord and a nod that held, then let go. They both watched the open gate and did not touch it.
They wrote the rule in the mud where feet would step it clean by morning:

-- Stakes lean with flow.
-- Brush to hum, not wall.
-- Basket mouth true; stone each side.
-- One gate always open.
-- Lift when the knocking speaks soft.
-- Thank with hands, not words.

Night cooled the water. The fence kept its shape and whispered. Sa-la lay on his side and watched the gate. "It bothers me," he said. "Good," Hakaka answered. "It bothers the river too. That keeps us both from sleeping stupid."
He slept. The river did what it does. The gate stayed open. The basket learned the sound of enough.

Mark: shallow pit · hot stones · mud lid
Vow: Heat tight; wait sweet.

They chose a place where wind came gentle and the ground rang when you kicked it. Hakaka pressed her heel, then her palm. "Dry," she said. "Good." La-la drew a circle with a stick, big enough for two hands of fish and a basket of roots. Sa-la started digging with a rib scraper. Taro took a flat stone and widened the sides. Ya-la brought leaves--broad, wet, green--and a bundle of thin branches.
The old woman sat on a folded cloak, knees up. "Make the mouth small," she said. "Heat runs when it sees sky." No one argued.

They gathered stones from the slope, not the river. La-la tapped each one with a pebble. Good ones rang. Bad ones thudded or cracked. "No water inside," she said. Sa-la tried to sneak in a smooth, pretty one from the stream. It popped in the small fire when they tested, a sharp report like a breaking tooth. He flinched, then nodded. Lesson held.

They lit a clean fire in the pit and fed it short sticks till the pit glowed. Stones went in on top, one by one with forked sticks. The fire hissed, then settled. "More," Hakaka said. "Stones first, hunger second." They kept feeding until the stones carried their own light.

While the pit heated, Ya-la washed the fish at the door stones from the weir. She ran her thumb along each belly, quick and kind. La-la peeled roots with the bone scraper, shaved them thin. Taro cracked two bulbs and set the cloves aside. The old woman handed him a packet of salt wrapped in leaf. "Little," she said. "Enough to wake, not to drown."
Sa-la cut green branches to make a grill. "Cross," La-la said, guiding his hands. "Let steam climb." He nodded, tongue at his teeth, and made a good grid.

When the stones glowed dull red, Hakaka raked the coals out to the side with a forked stick and a flat board. The pit breath was a hot fist. She waited a count till the air stopped biting. "Fast burns," she said. "We want slow."

They lined the pit with wet leaves. Steam puffed. Sa-la laughed at the sound and then kept his face out of it. Fish went down first, bellies stuffed with sliced root and the small cloves. More leaves. Thin cuts of meat from the last of the deer. More leaves. Taro poured a handful of water around the edge. It hissed and smelled like clean earth. "For breath," he said, and no one told him he was showing off.

They laid the green grill over the leaves and set a mud lid on top--clay mixed quick with straw and scraped with a rib to make it thin and strong. La-la sealed the edges with the heel of her hand. "Tight," she said. "Let the heat do the walking, not the wind."
"Vent," the old woman said, tapping the lid. Hakaka poked one small hole with a stick. A thin thread of steam rose and wandered. "Good," she said. "Draw."

Sa-la reached for the lid after the first finger of smell found him. Hakaka caught his wrist. "You want hot smoke and no dinner," she said. He pulled back and stood with his hands on the back of his neck. He faced away, breathing the good hurt.

They waited without talking. Wind shifted. The vent steamed steady, then thinner. La-la crouched and put her ear to the lid. "It talks softer," she said. The old woman nodded. "When the pot stops complaining," she said, "the food has learned its lesson."

Taro fidgeted. Ya-la handed him a stick. "Mark the wait," she said. He scratched short lines in the dirt by the pit, one for each count of a slow song. When he had ten, she put her palm over his. "Another five," she said. He exhaled like a pipe going cold and drew them.

Rain tried and failed. The sky had nothing serious in it. Sa-la checked the vent again and again and then made himself step back three paces so he wouldn’t touch what would hurt him. La-la stood where she could stop him if he forgot.

When the steam thinned to nothing and the lid smelled like clean clay, Hakaka lifted one edge with a forked stick. No blast. Good sign. She pried and set the lid aside on two stones. Steam rose lazy. The leaves nearest the lid were dark and sweet. Taro closed his eyes and smiled without showing teeth. Sa-la grinned full and didn’t hide it.

They pulled leaves away with sticks, not fingers. "Hot remembers," Ya-la said. Fish came out whole, flesh sliding from bones with no argument. Meat had the shine that means done. The roots were soft and carried the smell of the cloves. La-la tested one slice between thumb and forefinger. It yielded and held. She nodded once, pleased small.

They set food on clean bark and gave the first piece to the old woman. She chewed slow, then faster. "Teeth can sit down," she said. "Good work." Sa-la laughed and almost clapped, then didn’t. Hakaka gave him a look that said you are seen.

They ate without hurry. No one spoke big words. Grease ran down Sa-la’s wrist and he licked it, then wiped the rest on his forearm and grinned at the streak. Ya-la handed him a damp scrap to finish the job. "Don’t feed flies," she said. He nodded and used it.

Across the river the scar-mouth woman lifted her head like a fox catching scent. She watched the smoke shape. The cliff-man raised a hand, palm out, as if to say good work or we smell you or both. Hakaka lifted the vent stick in answer and turned it in a circle. The woman nodded once and went back to her own fire.

When they were full enough, they packed the bones tight and set them to boil in a small pot to make tomorrow honest. "Fat first," the old woman reminded. Ya-la skimmed a little for her cup. "Quiet throat," she said, and the old woman pretended not to smile.

Sa-la wanted to dig the pit out and build it better right then. La-la put a hand on his shoulder. "Hot rocks crack when you hurry them," she said. "Let them sleep." He scuffed his heel and then sat with his palms on his knees, eyes finding the vent hole again like it owed him something. "It will be there," Hakaka said. "If not, we’ll make it again. Easier next time."

They let the lid dry by the small fire, turning it once so it wouldn’t warp. Taro chipped a notch in the rim to seat the vent stick better. Ya-la scratched a small mark on the lid’s top--a circle with one short line--so anyone would know where to lift and where to leave alone.
When the pot of bones was set on the coals, they wrote the rules in ash and said them through, each to hold one:

-- Stones from slope, not river.
-- Heat the pit till stones carry light.
-- Leaves wet, layers thin.
-- Lid thin; edges sealed; one vent.
-- Wait past the first good smell.
-- Sticks for lifting; fingers last.
-- First piece to the one who needs soft.
-- Bones to tomorrow.

Night brought a thin chill. The old woman’s cough was small. Sa-la lay on his back and watched sparks drift up like insects that knew where to go. "We made a small earth with weather," he said, quiet. La-la grunted. "We kept it from lying," she said.

Before sleep, Hakaka used the last heat of the pit to dry two new cords and warm the damp in the robe where seams had argued with the day. She pressed her palm to the lid and left no mark. "Warm holds longer when it has a home," she said.
In the morning, the stones would still be warm enough to start the day’s fire without smoke in the eyes. They would not have to beg the neighbors for a coal. That was a kind of wealth.
They slept with good bellies and clean hands. The pit kept a low promise under the dirt.

Mark: V of stakes · brush fence · basket throat
Vow: Take only what returns; leave a door.

Morning gave them a cold river with a slow shoulder. Hakaka walked the bank with her hands behind her back, counting without numbers. "Here," she said. "Bottom is firm. Current is honest." La-la squatted and pushed a stake down with both palms. It bit and stood. "Good ground."

Taro carried a bundle of cut willow, ends clean and sharp. Sa-la dragged brush thatched with last year’s leaves. Ya-la brought twine and a basket they had woven for this. The old woman sat on a rock with the sun on her back. She did not talk much when there was work that needed breath.

Across the water the scar-mouth woman stood with her boy. The cliff of a man came later with stakes over his shoulder like spare ribs. He looked at Hakaka, then at the open river. He set one stake in the shallows on his side, nothing more. A question in wood.

Hakaka stepped into the cold up to the knee and gasped through her teeth. "Edges," she said. "We give the river an easier place to go." La-la nodded. They set the first line: stakes in a row, slanting downstream, a hand apart. Sa-la hammered with a round stone, eager, missing once and bruising knuckles. He hissed, then kept going. "Hit your own hand last," La-la said without looking.

They bent the line into a long V that pointed into the flow. The open end faced upstream. Brush went between stakes, butt to the current, thin at first so water could learn the path. "Not a wall," Ya-la said. "A guide."

Across the way, the woman mirrored them. The cliff-man set his stakes slow, straight, sure. The boy watched both banks at once. When the two Vs reached toward each other like careful hands, they left a gap where the points nearly met. Hakaka lifted a flat stone and set it there in the shallows. "Door," she said. "We take less to take longer."
Taro frowned. "We need fish now." Hakaka didn’t argue. She touched his wrist, two beats. "Now and later." He looked away, then nodded once, not happy and not fighting.

They tied the basket to the narrow throat of the V on their side, mouth toward the gap. Ya-la checked the lashings twice, then a third time as if her fingers could smell their weakness. "If it pulls free," she said, "we feed the river a day’s work." Sa-la tied another line from the basket to a root on shore. He tested by leaning his weight and letting it take him a little. The line held. He grinned without showing teeth.

They fed brush into the fence until the river’s voice changed--a lower, steady talk. Drift that would have swung past now nosed the slant and slid along it like a tired animal choosing a path. "Let it tire," La-la said. "Then ask."

The first fish came accidental--a silver back bumping the brush and flicking through the gap into the basket like it had decided that way itself. The basket shook once and stilled. Sa-la whooped. Hakaka lifted a hand and he made the sound smaller and kept it in his chest.

Ya-la pulled the basket in slow. She didn’t lift it. She turned it toward her knee and let the water drain, then raised it enough to see. Two fish, one small, one big as a forearm. She gave the small one to the river through the door. The big one she knocked clean with a flat stone. "One to teach the others," the old woman said. No one argued.
The cliff-man watched that and did the same on his side. He took two, let one go. The scar-mouth woman looked at Hakaka and gave a small nod that said we understand the same thing.

They worked the fence in short bursts. Brush wants to float; they pinned it with thin cross-branches woven through like stitches. Sa-la wanted to stuff the gaps tight. La-la pulled some out with two sharp tugs. "Fast flood, fence goes. Loose flood, fence lives." She left places that would tear away clean instead of dragging the whole weir to the sea.

Midday, the current strengthened. A log came down like a bad idea, rolling slow with a hidden speed. Hakaka spotted it and pointed. "Hands off." They stepped back. The log struck the slant, pressed, then the loose ties broke as they were meant to, giving it a straight line out and away. The fence looked injured but not ruined. Sa-la swore soft and honest. "We built the break in," Ya-la said. "Or the river builds it for us."

They repaired what tore. Taro split new willow with a bone wedge and fed La-la lengths with clean, white insides. He worked with his mouth shut, which was new. The old woman slept a little with her chin on her chest and woke to say, "Leave a stone marker where the door is. Night remembers poorly." Sa-la set three flat stones in a line, small to big, just upstream of the gap. He set them twice, because the first time they looked clever and not clear.

By late light, fish gathered like thoughts. They came along the slant, turned at the V, and tried the door. Some learned it and slid away. Some made the basket shake and stay. Ya-la pulled at a steady pace, not greedy. "We take what we can clean today," she said. "No rot."

Across the river the boy copied Sa-la’s stone marks. He got the pattern wrong the first time, big to small. Sa-la laughed, then stopped and made the motion with his hands--small to big like a road into a narrow place. The boy fixed it and raised his chin, pleased. The scar-mouth woman pretended not to see either of them.

The cliff-man brought over a length of rope made of something darker than reed. He held it out across the gap on a long pole. Hakaka pushed their basket line toward him with a branch. Lines touched, tangled, then found a way to coil around each other where the current wouldn’t worry them. The two weirs leaned toward being one without stepping into each other’s soil. "With," Ya-la said under her breath, and the word felt right.

They ate while they worked--thin strips cut quick and swallowed without ceremony. The old woman chewed slow and then handed the last piece to Sa-la. He started to hand it back. She pushed his fingers closed. "Grow," she said. He did.

At dusk, they opened the door wider and left the basket empty. "Night is for teaching," Hakaka said. "Day is for taking." Sa-la didn’t like it, but he set the stones so the gap was clear even in dim light. Taro stood with his hands in the river and felt the pull and the let-go. He closed his eyes like he was fixing the shape inside him.

They wrote the rules in ash and wiped them flat when the mouths had said them true: set stakes slanting downstream; weave loose enough to tear clean; leave a door and mark it; basket at the throat, not the mouth; take what you can use fresh; let some go always; fix what the river teaches you to fix; no work alone in fast water.

Rain came thin and cold. They covered the fish with wet leaves while they cleaned, guts for the dogs far from camp, skins hung high. Sa-la slipped once on the slick rock, caught himself with both hands, and laughed at the sound he made. La-la bumped his shoulder. "Feet think better when fed," she said, and shoved a piece into his mouth.
They slept to the sound of water practicing its lesson against their work.

At first light the door stones were still where he’d left them. Sa-la lifted the basket and found it full enough to make his shoulders speak. He braced his feet and did not ask for help. Hakaka watched and didn’t step in until he needed it, which he didn’t, and that became a fact he would carry.

Across the river, the scar-mouth woman lifted her basket at the same time and set it down in mirror. She held up two fingers, then touched her breastbone and pointed to the gap. Two left, mine. Hakaka held up three, touched the basket, and pointed to the door. Three left, ours. They both nodded. A law without a voice, agreed anyway.

Before they closed for the day, Hakaka picked the smallest fish from their catch, still bright. She bent to the door and let it slip through her fingers into the slow seam. It flashed and was gone. Sa-la looked at her hand. "Why that one?" "So the river tells that story too," she said.
The old woman stood with help and shuffled to the bank. She looked down at the V and the door and the neat stones. "You made a mouth," she said. "Teach it to speak kind and it will feed long."

They banked brush at the weak places, left the door clear, and tied the basket high. The cliff-man put his palm to his chest and then to the river and then to the weir like he was stamping all three together. Ya-la did the same, and they both smiled, small and tired and not at each other.

When they walked home, Sa-la kept looking over his shoulder at the stones marking the door. "Will they stay?" he asked. "They’ll move," La-la said. "So will we." He nodded. He would come at dawn and set them right again. He already knew the right places like he knew his own hands.

That night they ate fish cooked on green sticks and laid on hot stones, and no one said there had been a better meal. The weir talked in the dark, low and steady. In the morning, it would talk again, and they would listen, and leave the door.

Mark: clay ring · draw-hole · cap
Vow: Heat likes tight; wait until wait turns sweet.

They chose a flat shoulder of ground out of the wind and not far from water. Hakaka knelt and pressed her palm to the dirt. "Hard enough," she said. "Not so hard the clay won’t bite." La-la nodded. "We build where feet won’t trip." She scratched a circle with a stick, big as her arms could make.

Taro brought shovel stones--the flat ones that cut earth if you ask right. Sa-la carried damp clay in a woven sling that leaked on his leg and made him look like he’d walked through a low river. Ya-la had sand in a basket and a small bag of salt. "A pinch keeps cracks from running," she said. The old woman watched with her lips thin, saving her breath. "Don’t make it pretty," she warned. "Make it strong."

They mixed clay with sand and a little salt under shade. La-la trod the heap with both feet until it answered her heel with a deep, close sound. Sa-la wanted to add more water. Ya-la stopped his hand. "Thirsty clay lies," she said. "It will drink and then sag." He left it and learned the patience in his neck.

They rolled the first rope of clay and laid it along the scratch, pressing it flat, then another coil on top, staggering the joins. The ring grew up from the ground like a slow snake sitting down. Taro smoothed the inner wall with a wet stone until it felt like a bowl. La-la left a narrow mouth on one side, low to the ground. "Feed here," she said. "Work from here. Smoke wants out the other way."

Hakaka marked a small, round hole opposite the mouth, a hand above the ground. "Draw," she said. She pushed a smooth stick through and left it there so the hole would keep its circle. "When breath goes in, fire gives back." The old woman almost smiled. "Teach it to breathe. Good."

They made a cap: a shallow dome the size of a big platter, with a rim that would sit over the ring’s mouth. Ya-la pressed a loop of reed into the cap’s top so you could lift it with a stick. Sa-la wanted to make a little bird on the top. La-la knocked the thought out of the clay with her thumb. "Later." He flushed, then laughed at himself and smoothed the smear. "Later," he said.

They let the ring rest in shade while they gathered fuel: finger-width sticks for heat, arm-thick for bank, chips for talk. Taro found a dead root heavy as a boy and cut it into rounds. Hakaka shook her head. "That is for overnight, not now." Taro lifted one piece anyway. "I like to know it’s waiting." Hakaka said nothing. She liked that too.

At dusk they fired the ring. Small bundle first, a thin fire that talked fast and light. Ya-la fed it like a hungry dog you don’t trust yet--often, little. The dampness came out of the clay in a fine sweat. Hairline lines showed, then closed again. "Don’t smile at it," La-la said to Sa-la when he grinned at the first lick of flame through the draw-hole. "It will remember your teeth and crack there." He shut his mouth and watched.

The dome cap dried near the heat, turning from dark to the color of baked bread. Sa-la tapped it with a stick. It answered low and true. "Not yet," Hakaka said. "It hasn’t learned how to hold." They let the ring eat for a long time, always feeding from the mouth, never starving it and never letting it rage. When the inner wall glowed a little like a warm stone at noon, Hakaka nodded. "Enough. We teach it food."

They set the cap over the mouth, leaving a finger’s gap at the bottom. Smoke gathered, looked for any foolish place to go, then learned the road of the draw-hole. The little plume lifted true. The old woman put her hand just inside the gap and winced, pleased. "Heat likes tight," she said. "You did not forget."

Sa-la put his nose near the gap. Hakaka flicked his ear without looking. He moved back a hand. "I was just smelling." "Smell later," La-la said. "Wait now." He waited, but his foot told the dirt a story.

Ya-la counted slow breaths. After forty, she lifted the cap a finger. Steam kissed her knuckles and did not bite. "Not yet," she said. After a while more, she lifted again. The round had gone from wet to dull to a small, honest color. The edge lifted with a whisper. La-la slid a stick under and turned it. It let go. "Now," La-la said, not with her mouth.

They ate the first flat with their fingers while it still complained about leaving the stone. It tasted of smoke and seed and something like the inside of a new bowl. Sa-la burned his tongue and did not spit; he chased the hurt with breath and pride. The old woman chewed slow, eyes wet but not from feeling. "It will keep," she said. "Make three more before sleep. Your morning selves will call you smart."

They learned the oven’s temper the next day. Too much wood too fast and the paste blistered and sulked. Too little and it lay asleep in the middle. "A good mouth and a good back," La-la said, tapping, listening. "We feed it like a child, and like a child it will tell us what sort of day it’s having."

The clay cracked once, a thin line from mouth toward the side. Sa-la saw it first and felt it with a finger he didn’t deserve. The line widened. "Sorry," he said out loud to no one and everyone. Ya-la pressed a paste of clay and ash into the cut while the wall was still warm. She spoke to the oven like she would to a baby that had worked too hard. "Hold, hold." It held. She left a thumbprint where the fix sat. "Now it remembers you," La-la said. "Don’t make it flattering."

In the afternoon the wind turned on them. Smoke sulked at the mouth and tried to crawl into eyes. Hakaka moved a basket and the old woman’s seat two steps to the left. "Wind door," she said. She knocked a reed screen together and set it so the mouth had a leeward ear. The change was small and the result was large; smoke learned manners again. "Door wants a leeward ear," La-la said, liking how it sounded because it was true.

The cliff of a man came at dusk with a bundle of split wood cut to wrist length. He set it down without stepping inside the circle of work. Hakaka walked the split pile with her eyes and then her hand, measuring without measuring. "That’s right," she said--two words he could carry. The scar-mouth woman held up a palm full of something the color of dusk. "River clay," Ya-la guessed. The woman nodded, tapped the crack-line on their oven, then her own hip, then the bundle. Shared problems; shared ways to fix them. They traded a flat round for a pinch of the smooth dark, wrapped in leaf.

Night came with a thin, hard cold. They banked the oven with a back wall of coals pulled in tight and the cap left breathing small. La-la dragged the biggest root round near. "Not inside," Hakaka said. "By the mouth. Let the oven remember heat but not choke on it." La-la obeyed and sat next to the warm clay like it was a small animal leaning against her for trust. Sa-la fell asleep with his head near the draw-hole, which ticked and sighed like a patient chest.

At dawn the cap still held a little hand of warmth. Ya-la blew through the hole and fed a handful of dry grass. A low glow answered and climbed the grass like a careful friend. "It kept," she said, and even the old woman made a sound you could count as pleased.

They made rules and wrote them in wet ash, then wiped them flat when all had said them true: build with sand in the clay; leave a draw-hole and keep it round; feed from the mouth, breathe through the back; cap down for keeping, lifted for turning; wait until the wait turns sweet; never leave it hot and alone; fix cracks when warm; don’t teach it your teeth.

On the third day Sa-la tried meat inside because patience had looked away. He thrust a strip too deep and too fast; fat spat and took to flame. Smoke turned harsh and the oven coughed. Hakaka grabbed his wrist and pulled his hand out before he cooked it. La-la closed the cap tight, then lifted it an inch and left the draw-hole wide. The harsh went out like a bad thought told no audience. Sa-la stood with his hand in cold clay at the river’s lip, eyes angry with himself. Ya-la came and smeared honey on the reddened skin; the bees had offered, and now the sweetness had a second job. "So it minds its manners," she said. He nodded, small. "I’ll mind mine." The old woman snorted. "News."

They found the oven could dry reeds, warm a sleeping stone, crisp the fat on a fish skin so it broke like good laughter. It could take wet from shoes, save coals for mornings, and give back the taste of yesterday’s smoke to today’s food so memory had a mouth-feel. "Story fire," Ya-la said once, very quiet, and no one called it a name again, but the name stayed anyway.

On a day of thin rain, steam rolled off the cap like breath in winter. Taro rubbed his hands, put the backs of his cold fingers against the clay rim, and closed his eyes as if listening. "I like a thing that holds," he said. "Even when the sky forgets us." Hakaka didn’t say she felt the same. She just fed the mouth with a length of split wood the cliff of a man had cut and set the cap neat, twice.

Before sleep, La-la ran her knuckles around the ring and found no loose talk in the wall. At the draw-hole she paused and didn’t poke a stick through. She looked and left it. "It breathes right," she said to the dirt, then lay down and rolled her shoulder until the day clicked out. The oven ticked to itself, keeping one small ember the color of a patient eye.

In the morning, flats warmed fast, fish took smoke proper, and no one burned a tongue. The old woman ate slow and watched the little plume at the draw-hole go steady. "I have cooked on worse mouths," she said. "Plenty worse." Hakaka touched the clay and felt it hold. "We can keep this," she said. "If we remember why we keep it tight--and when to open." Sa-la nodded like the rule had a place to live in him now. He stayed long enough to finish his flat, then ran errands without being told.

By evening the oven had become part of the ground the way a path becomes more path the more you use it. It was ugly and perfect. It remembered hands. It warmed what asked. It kept a little of yesterday for tomorrow, and didn’t brag.

Mark: V of stones · reed gate · spill-way
Vow: Let the river choose the point; leave a door.

They walked the shallows at first light. Hakaka stepped heel then toe to feel the floor. La-la watched the way the water leaned. Taro tested with a pole and nodded when the tip kissed gravel, not silt. "Here," he said. "Bottom rises. Banks come close. Fish push hard past this place."

Across the water the scar-mouth woman stood with the boy and the cliff of a man. She raised a hand. Hakaka raised one back and pointed at the narrowing. The woman looked left, looked right, and tapped the same place with her foot. Good.
They scratched a V on each side with sticks, point downstream. "Mouth here," La-la said. "Wings there and there." She set the first stone and listened with her palm. "Flat on flat. No wobble."

They carried stones, not the biggest--honest ones that could be held. The cliff of a man took larger, set them like he’d been waiting to do it. Sa-la tried to stack fast. La-la knocked one down with two fingers. "No fast if it falls," she said. "We stack low and wide. River will try to move what is proud."

Ya-la cut reeds where they grew thick and green. The boy cut too, keeping his blue scrap out of the water. They wove a square--tight at first, then tighter when Sa-la tested it and the weave gaped. "Gate," Ya-la said. She tied two cross sticks at the top for a carry hand. The woman showed a knot Sa-la didn’t know. He learned it with his fingers, twice, until it stayed without a thought.

By noon the wings reached most of the way from each bank. The point of the V waited empty. "Spill-way there," Hakaka said, tapping a low run where big water could pass without tearing the work. "We like to live after rain."

They pressed mud between stones where the water tried to talk through. "Press and feel," La-la said. "When your thumb doesn’t find a mouth, move on." Taro packed gravel at the feet of the wings so the current would push on ground, not under. The cliff of a man pressed his weight along the V and watched the water change tone. He grunted once. Approval.
They set the reed gate at the point, tied to two stakes. It hung in the flow and pushed back true. Sa-la smiled. The gate pushed his smile flat and then let it up again.

"Rule," Hakaka said, and spoke it to both banks. "We leave a door." She lifted two stones from the very end and set them aside. A gap the width of her hand shone. "Small ones pass. Breeders pass. We eat long, not just loud."
The old woman had come as far as the bank allowed and sat on a dry log. "You build a hand to catch water," she said. "You will learn what it slaps."

They tried at dusk when fish nose hardest. Ya-la set a string of pebbles on a flat rock--three for first check, five for second, seven for last. "We go when the shadow reaches each stone," she said. Sa-la wanted to bend the plan. Hakaka looked once. He didn’t.

At the first check the gate held. A single small fish nosed the weave and slid through the gap like a thought. "Good," La-la said. "Door works." Taro lifted the gate by its cross sticks. The wings coughed two finger-length fish into his basket. He dropped them back and said nothing. Ya-la saw and tucked that away.

Second check: the water had found a soft seam under the left wing. It whispered there and took a handful of mud. "It always will," La-la said. They packed it tight with gravel and heel, then set a stone that fit the hole like it had been waiting to be used. The cliff of a man watched the fix and mirrored it on his side. No talk.

At the last check the river had brought more. The gate quivered with life. Sa-la lifted too fast and the square bucked. Two fish leapt and were gone. He flushed. La-la put her palm on the cross sticks with his. "Together. Up slow. Let the heads find stillness." They lifted, steady. Taro slid the flat basket under and pulled the gate over it. The fish slapped the wicker and stayed.

They counted out loud so no boast could change the number. Ten fish. La-la pointed to three with swollen bellies and let them go. Hakaka pointed to two thin ones and let them go too. "Keep seven," she said. "We eat now and not hate ourselves later."
Across the water the woman counted as well and made her own cuts. She held one fish up until Hakaka held one too, then let it go. They laughed once, not loud.

They hung the catch from a forked pole and walked back with the gate under Sa-la’s arm. The boy across did the same. The cliff of a man came last, hands empty, eyes on the way the water pulled at the outer stones. He moved one with his foot and stood longer to see if the line held. It did.

At the fire they cleaned fish fast. Ya-la rubbed a smear of salt inside each belly, slid a strip of green along the spine, and set them by the oven’s mouth for smoke and heat. The smell made the old woman’s face soften before her words did. "About time," she said, which for her meant well done.
They ate and left bones for the dogs well away from sleeping. Sa-la reached for a crisp tail. Hakaka shook her head once. He put it with the others high out of reach. The lesson was old. It held.

Next day the river rose a thumb. The spill-way took the push and saved the wings. In the afternoon a heavy branch came down and struck the right side hard. It shifted the outside three stones. Taro saw it first and shouted. Sa-la ran and braced the gap with his body without thinking and took the hit in his thigh. La-la and the cliff of a man set stones back while the branch jammed against Sa-la and used him as a post. When the line was true again, Hakaka pushed the branch off with a pole and caught Sa-la by his belt before the river took him. He stood up slow and did not talk for a while. Later he admitted the river had bitten him purple. The old woman gave him a look that said good and stupid at once. He took both.

Toward evening they found a handful of small ones trapped in a little pocket behind a wobbly stone. Ya-la put them back. She set her palm over the pocket and felt the pull. "This is a bad mouth," she said. "It will eat small fish for no reason." They filled it with gravel until it went quiet.

They made more rules and kept them short: check three times then leave it; lift the gate with two hands; count in the open; let small and heavy-bellied go; stand out of the spill when rain thinks loud; fix what leaks before you sleep. Hakaka pressed each with a stick into wet sand, then smeared the sand flat when all had said them. Taro never looked away while she did it.

On the third day the cliff of a man walked to the water with a small bundle. He set a stone where their line was weakest and tapped it twice, then set the bundle on the rock and stepped back. Ya-la went to the edge and used the reed line to drag it across. In it: three short stakes, sharpened right, and a coil of bark cord you could trust. Hakaka put a small pouch of salt in the bundle and sent it back. No one clapped.
That night the weir held a soft song. Sa-la lay on his back and listened. "We made a place the river speaks to," he said.
"We made a place the river agrees with," Hakaka said. "That’s different."
He nodded like he felt the truth of it in his bones.

Before sleep La-la ran her knuckles along the stones one by one. She found a loose one and worked it tight without calling anyone. When she came to the gap at the point she didn’t touch it. She just looked and left it. "One goes on purpose," she said to herself, and liked the shape of that in her mouth.

In the morning the wings were still where hands had put them. The gate lifted without fuss. Five fish, kept honest by what they’d let pass. The old woman ate slow and looked at the river. "I have seen worse laws," she said. "I’ve seen plenty worse."
Hakaka laid her palm on the wet stone and felt it hold. "This one we can keep," she said. "If we remember why we leave the door."

Mark: stone oval · clay dome · draw-hole
Vow: Heat likes tight; wait until the wait turns sweet.

They chose a place out of the wind where the ground held firm. Hakaka tapped her heel and listened. "Here," she said. "Dry under the skin." La-la scratched an oval in the dust. Taro carried stones, flat and heavy, and set them edge to edge until the line was a ring.

Ya-la brought clay from the bed in a wet cloth. Sa-la shredded dry grass and mixed it in. The clay took the chaff and held better. "Rib first," La-la said. She bent three green sticks and planted their ends inside the ring, crossing them to make a low spine.

They smeared clay over the ribs a handful at a time. The dome rose slow and honest. Sa-la tried to make it smooth. La-la pressed his hand away. "No pretty," she said. "Tight." She pinched the seams shut with a wet thumb. Hakaka left a mouth just big enough for her forearm and, above it, pressed a small hole for the smoke to pull. "Mouth low, draw high," she said. "Fire likes a path."
The old woman sat on a flat rock and watched the clay darken as the sun took water out of it. "If it falls," she said, "duck."

When the dome held its own weight, they lit a small fire inside--thin sticks, then thicker. The clay steamed and sweated. A line cracked at the crown. Sa-la hissed. Ya-la was already there with a slurry and a scrap of wet cloth. She rubbed the crack until it closed. "It will crack again," she said. "We will close it again."

They fed the fire until the dome turned the color of dry bread. La-la held her palm near the mouth and counted. "Too hot to count to two," she said. "Good." They let the flame settle and pushed char aside. The inside glowed a quiet red.

Taro wanted to work fast. He cut tubers into fists and wrapped them in clay leaves, a trick they’d learned by mistake. Sa-la cleaned a fish the river owed them and laid it on wetted leaves with a reed of salt rubbed along the belly. Ya-la brought a flat pan of damp earth and pressed thin cakes from pounded seeds. Hakaka pinched a little hole in each--"so it breathes and doesn’t blister wrong."

They set a bed of wet greens on the floor, slid the food in with the end of a flat stick, and capped the mouth with a stone they’d saved for this. La-la packed clay around the stone so no breath leaked. Only the draw-hole smoked, thin and steady.
Taro crouched and put his ear to the dome. "I hear it talking," he said.
"It’s steam," Ya-la said. "It stops when the inside turns right."
"Until the wait turns sweet," Hakaka said. She set a stick in the sand near the mouth, leaned to the same angle as the sun. "When the shadow touches the stone, we look."
The old woman coughed and laughed at once. "You made a pot you cannot pick up," she said. "About time."

While they waited, La-la shaped a second stone to fit the mouth better. "The first one is a little loose," she said.
