The river had eaten half the bank overnight. Mud slumped where they used to stand. Everyone was wet and short on sleep.
"La-la, hold this," Hakaka said, passing her the line. "Not hero-tight. Hands alive."
"My hands are already alive," La-la muttered. The rope burns on her palms had opened again. She didn’t show them, but the sting made her jaw hard.

Ya-la crouched near the edge, chewing a short tail of twine she’d meant to trim. She stopped when she noticed herself, spat the fiber into the grass, and wiped her mouth with the back of her wrist. "Current’s faster than yesterday," she said. "Middle looks ugly."
Sa-la stamped his feet like a colt. "I can throw the pouch farther now." He lifted his gourd, proud. It still leaked. He’d plugged the hole with a wad of chewed bark and felt very clever.

"No throws," Hakaka said. "We ferry it. Slow." She pointed to the float: a reed bundle the size of a hand, a leather pouch tied on top, a strip of bright grass knotted as a flag. "First tug means they see it. Second means they answer. If it snags, we don’t dive. We cut and try again."
"Because we don’t drown for a message," Ya-la finished, too fast. She stared at the water and rubbed her forearm where old scratches turned pale in the cold.
La-la set her feet, line looped around her waist. "Ready."

They eased the float into the water. Hakaka fed slack inch by inch. The bundle bobbed, turned, and the river took it sideways, toward a tangle of roots. La-la shifted her weight. The bank under her gave a lazy sigh and slid a hand’s breadth.
"Back," Hakaka said. La-la swore, just loud enough. She was tired of being careful.

Sa-la leaned to see better. His heel crushed the lip of mud; the edge dropped and he went to his knee with a splash. Cold water hit his ribs. His face twisted--shock first, then shame. His hand flew to his belt. "My knife!"

"Forget it," Hakaka snapped. "Stand up." She grabbed his shoulder and hauled. He was heavier than yesterday; he’d been stealing extra roasted roots when he thought no one saw. She filed that away for later.
"I can get it," he said, wild-eyed, pointing at the brown blur in the water.
He moved, teeth clenched. Water streamed from his tunic. He glared at the river as if it had insulted him.
The float caught on a hidden stick. The bright grass flag quivered and stopped. Ya-la sucked air through her teeth. "Snag."

Hakaka felt the line with her knuckles. The tug told her exactly nothing she wanted to hear. "Hold. I’ll work it." She edged the cord left, then right, feeding a little slack, lifting, lowering. Sometimes this worked. Today the river said no.
"We have the day," Hakaka said, but not as a proverb. Just a reminder. "We don’t have another pouch."

"We have mine," Ya-la said, too quickly. Her fingers went to the small leather bag at her neck. She didn’t untie it. She looked at the water again, then at her bag. The conflict showed on her face plain as sunlight.
Hakaka pretended not to see, to give her room to choose.
"Not ours," Ya-la whispered. "Look--downstream. It tore." A slice of leather flapped. Two of the beads that marked "need" were gone. The message now read like a stammer.
"Half of something," Hakaka said. "Which is worse." She felt the small, hateful press of fear under her ribs and put her palm flat on the ground until it passed.
"It snagged before you fell," La-la said. "Your fault is being loud and wet."
Ya-la flinched at the sharpness. "Stop." She pulled the thong of her neck pouch over her head with both hands. Her fingers shook. "Take mine."
"That’s your father’s," La-la said, softer now. "You don’t have to--"
"I do," Ya-la said. "I can make another. I can’t make another chance."

Hakaka met her eyes, held them a breath. "Thank you." She kept the words small. She cut the old float loose and reeled it back. "Sa-la, wring your clothes. You shiver, you go sit by the embers, no noise."
"Noise," La-la said under her breath, but she handed him a scrap of dry cloth anyway.

They worked fast. Hakaka tied the new pouch tighter than was comfortable and double-wrapped the reed bundle. La-la shifted the anchor point back from the soft edge and tested it with her whole body. Ya-la stood very still and didn’t look at the place where the bank had slid. She tied the bright grass higher, for sight.
"Ready," Ya-la said, and she was. She tucked her trembling hand into her belt where no one could see it.
"Ready," Sa-la said, muffled by the cloth he was using to dry his chest. He tried to sound older.

They eased the second float onto the current. It skated along the smoother line Hakaka picked with her hand. Halfway across, it drifted toward the same tangle. Hakaka breathed out slow, shifted the angle by two fingers, and felt the line lift free.
"Eat after we finish," La-la said to no one, and to her stomach, which had chosen that moment to complain. "I’m going to skin my own hands if this fails," she added, half prayer, half threat.
"Don’t," Ya-la said, a quick flash of humor. "They’re useful."
The float nosed into calmer water on the far side. Hakaka watched the bright strip wink between ripples and felt the small pull she’d been waiting for.
"Please," Sa-la whispered to the river, to whoever was there, to himself.

They waited. The cold crawled up their calves. A gull screamed, unhelpful. La-la’s shoulders began to quiver with the effort of holding steady. Ya-la’s jaw clicked as she tried not to chew another line-end. Sa-la put the gourd to his lips and blew without thinking. The patched hole turned his breath into a wet, flat trumpet. It was horrible.
"Keep it," Hakaka said, surprising herself. "If they’re listening, let them know we’re stubborn."
Sa-la’s eyes lit. He blew again, longer. The sound was ugly and alive. Across the river, something moved--low and quick in the trees. The line twitched.
"Two," Hakaka echoed. She let herself breathe fully for the first time that morning.
La-la sagged and then recovered as the bank softened again beneath her heel. "Pull or wait?" she asked, asking Hakaka but also asking the day to be simple for once.
"Wait for the tie," Hakaka said. "They’ll add their cord." She spoke like she’d done this a thousand times. She had not. She made herself sound like a person whose plans worked.
Another small pull came, then a slow, steady weight. The far side was paying attention.
"Now," Hakaka said. She and La-la drew the line back, hand over hand, easy, no jerks. Ya-la leaned in to watch the knots. Sa-la hopped from foot to foot, forgetting he was cold.
The float came home with a new cord knotted to it, rough fiber from a plant Hakaka didn’t recognize. The pouch was still sealed. Ya-la’s breath fogged it as she reached. She paused. "May I?"

Ya-la opened it. Inside: three small pebbles, smooth and dark, and a twist of dried meat. The pebbles said "we saw, we heard, we will come when the water drops." The meat said "someone over there understands hunger."

La-la laughed once, a short bark, then wiped her face hard with the back of her wrist like she was scolding her own eyes. "Good. Good." She flexed her hands and hissed at the sting. "I hate this river," she added, sincere and human.

Sa-la blew the trumpet again, softer now, like a thanks. It still sounded awful. Ya-la actually clapped her hands over her ears before she laughed. Hakaka let herself lean against a rock and feel her heart steady under her palm. For three breaths, she let the old fear stand in the doorway and look around. Then she shut the door gently. Not banished--just not in charge.
"Wrap your hands," she told La-la. "Ya-la, keep that cord; we’ll learn it. Sa-la, you’re on fire watch when we get back. And you owe the cook two roots for the noise tax."

They moved. The river kept its own thoughts. The bank creaked one last time as if reminding them who owned what. On the path home, Sa-la tried not to shiver and failed. La-la complained about mud in her boots and did not stop complaining. Ya-la walked in the middle and held the new cord like a promise she hadn’t made out loud.
They were quieter than usual. Not solemn, just tired. The stew would be thin. The message was enough. For a morning like this, enough was plenty.

Morning thinned the mist over the river. The current moved like a muscle under skin, steady, a little arrogant. Hakaka stood ankle-deep in the chill and let it bite. She would rather have waited for sun, but the bank had slumped in the night--fresh cuts in the mud like teeth marks--and she wanted a line across before the next bite.
La-la hauled the reed rope to her hip and tested the first loop. "It’ll hold," she said, too quickly.
"Will it?" Hakaka asked, softer than doubt, but not softer than care.
La-la’s mouth tightened. She tugged again, slower this time, listening with her hands. The loop answered with a clean pull. "Now it will."

Ya-la opened her pouch and tipped pebbles into her palm. She always chose the warm, round ones and rubbed them when she thought no one watched. "I’m using three," she said. "One for danger, one for food, one for talk." She hesitated and slipped in a fourth. "And one for please," she added, almost embarrassed.
Sa-la came down from the bank with a little clay gourd, still smelling of smoke. "It floats," he announced. "I tested it in the wash bowl. Mostly."
He set it in the shallows. It bobbed, proud as a chick, then rolled on its side and took a mouthful of river, coughing like a bad liar.

La-la laughed through her nose. Ya-la tried not to. Sa-la flushed and snatched it back. "I made another," he said, producing a second gourd with a wavy seam. "This one floats always." He could not meet Hakaka’s eyes.

Hakaka did not reach for the gourd yet. Her fingers found the inside of her wrist, the old loop scar there. She hadn’t noticed herself doing that in a long time. She lowered her hand. "We’ll use both," she said. "If the river wants a toy, let it steal the first, not the last."

They anchored a line to a stout root and threw the reed across. The first throw fell short and plopped uselessly. La-la swore--nothing poetic, just the old, ugly word for a stubbed toe--and shook out her shoulders. "Again." The second throw caught a crooked branch on the far side. La-la whooped, then pretended she hadn’t.

Ya-la tied the message pouch with the four pebbles. She chewed the knot once, a habit that made La-la wince. "It’s how I think," Ya-la said, without looking up. Her hand trembled; she tucked it under the rope until it forgot.
Sa-la clipped his second gourd to the line as a float. "Don’t pull yet," he told the river, as if the river listened. He glanced at Hakaka. "Can I…?"

They eased the pouch into the current. The gourd took the weight and bobbed obediently. The line whispered. The message nosed out, then, suddenly, the near bank slumped another fistful and the line sagged. Water grabbed the pouch and dragged it sideways.
"Hold!" La-la grunted, digging heels into slime. The rope burned her palms; she swore again, louder.

"The snag!" Ya-la cried. A submerged branch hooked the pouch. The gourd tilted. Sa-la lunged, and Hakaka’s heart did a small, old thing she didn’t let out of its room very often. She found herself breathing too fast, like a girl, and hated that she cared what it looked like. Then she didn’t care.

"Back," she snapped, voice sharp enough to cut. "Not you. You’re too light--me." She stepped into the deeper water. It swallowed her calves, then her knees. Cold shot up her bones. She loved the hurt--because it returned her to her hands.

She worked along the line, one fist at a time, feeling the talk of the current through her knuckles. The snag tugged like a stubborn child. "Give," she murmured, to no one and to everything. She rocked the pouch forward, back, forward, back. It slipped free with a shy jerk. She nearly laughed from relief and bit it down.
On shore, La-la’s arms shook. Ya-la mouthed a prayer to no god in particular, just to the habit of trying again. Sa-la hopped from foot to foot, desperate to help and desperate not to disobey.

"Now," Hakaka said, and they drew the line. Slow at first, then faster as the current relented. The pouch skimmed past the snag’s reach and sailed to the far bank, where it lodged in a wedge of roots like a bird in a nest.

They waited. Waiting always took longer than doing. A crow landed near the pouch and cocked its head, clearly considering a career in literacy. Ya-la threw a pebble--not a message pebble, a useless one--and the crow, offended, left.

Hunger arrived like a late guest and sat down in everyone’s stomachs. La-la scratched her arm and muttered about bread. Sa-la announced he had to pee and did, loudly, behind a bush. Ya-la found a stale seed in her pocket and almost ate it, then pressed it into the mud instead. "Grow, please," she whispered, which made Hakaka smile despite herself.

Across the river, nothing happened. Then the pouch twitched. A small animal must have nosed it, or the current shifted--no, the knot turned; the whole bundle pivoted a quarter turn and stilled. La-la frowned. "That’s nothing."
Hakaka watched the angle of the line where it met the water. It changed. Barely, but enough. "Pull," she said.

They drew the rope back hand over hand. The gourd came first, then the pouch, dripping and twice as heavy. Ya-la snatched it and opened the knot with teeth and fingers. Inside, their three pebbles tumbled out--danger, food, talk--and a fourth joined them. Not "please." A flat, dark stone with a new scratch on it: a crooked arrow.
"Who?" La-la asked, but her voice had lost its hardness. The arrow pointed downstream, toward the bend where the bank liked to pretend it was stone until a heavy night taught it otherwise.
Hakaka tasted fear and found it useful. "Downriver," she said. "We go with bread, not with pride."

Ya-la tied the arrow-stone back into the pouch with the food pebble. "Trade," she said, as if naming it made it safer. La-la wiped her palms on her thighs, embarrassed by the raw patches there, and tightened the anchor knot anyway.
Sa-la held up the first gourd, the one the river had laughed at. He stuck a thin reed through its belly and blew. It made a ridiculous, wet trumpet. Everyone stared at him.
"What?" he said, grinning despite himself. "If they’re downstream, they should hear us."

The sound was so ugly that even the crow croaked approval. Ya-la laughed first, helplessly, hand on her ribs. La-la tried to keep a straight face and failed. Hakaka let herself laugh last, because someone had to be last, and because the sound shook the cold out of her bones.

When they packed to go, she checked the line one more time. Habit, yes. But also love, which was the habit under all the other ones. She looked at her children--impatient, careful, blazing--and felt the old worry return and take a different shape: not a weight, a handle.
"Downriver," she said. "Eat while we walk. If anyone falls in, we fish them out before we argue whose fault it was."
"Especially you," La-la said, and ruffled his hair hard enough to make him yelp.

They lifted the rope, shouldered the gourds, and stepped into the path that would become a road because they decided to walk it more than once. The river kept talking behind them, pleased with itself. The gourd squeaked when Sa-la squeezed it by accident, and Ya-la threatened to throw it to the crow unless he kept it quiet. Hakaka looked back only once, at the far bank where the pouch had turned. She did not know who had scratched the arrow. She did not need to--yet.
"Small enough to cross a river," Hakaka said. Then they went.
Night leans on the grass. The shelter holds its breath. Hakaka kneels at the mouth and lets her palm speak to the robe: be still. The fabric listens. Cold travels under the door like a thin animal.

La-la stands where the reeds become rope. She tests the loop with bare fingers--find, then twist; twist, then test. The fibers answer with a faint rasp. She smiles without teeth. A good knot doesn’t brag.

Ya-la returns from the river with a pebble warm from her mouth. News has weight. She sets it in Hakaka’s hand and tilts her head to the wind. "Meat on four legs," she breathes. "Hungry, not angry." The wind agrees in the grass.

Sa-la squats over a coal sleeping in clay. He strokes the lid once--promise, not flame. His eyes shine like ideas he is not allowed to try. "Not yet," Hakaka whispers. He nods, a small sun obedient in his bowl.

The sound comes: a click swallowed by the door. Not panic. Three breaths. On the first they bend their knees. On the second La-la shifts the loop a thumb’s width down to where paws would choose. On the third Hakaka gives the robe her weight and the entrance gives the visitor nothing.

A nose tests the circle. A paw commits. The loop answers. Not a snare to choke--Hakaka hates that hunger--but a sudden tug sideways, a rude truth: not here. The beast scrapes, angry at geometry, then huffs off into scrub. For a while the grass keeps talking after it is gone.

Knees unlock. Laughter arrives late and low, not to mock but to oil the hinge between fear and breath. "Our guest admired your knot," Ya-la says. La-la bows to the door like a priest to a clean floor. Sa-la lifts his lid a finger’s width and grins at the tiny blue waiting there. Then closes it. Discipline tastes like smoke you don’t swallow.

They count costs. The loop bit the reed too deep; a strand split where it met the peg. Hakaka rubs ash into her palms, the grey of yesterday’s fire. "Memory for grip." Ash roughens, reed listens, fingers learn. She shows the split to the girls. "Cracks draw maps. Follow them to where we mend next."

A faint drip from the roof lies through its teeth. La-la taps the seam. "Not a leak--just shy clay." She folds a smear over it, checks again. "Second look saves breakfast." Ya-la nods toward the night. "And sometimes a life." Their eyes go to Sa-la. He pretends not to notice and watches his small star instead.

"Again," Hakaka says. Practice is a broom; it keeps luck from piling up. La-la resets the circle, lower, cleaner. She tugs until the peg sings. Grip before twist. Test before trust. Ya-la shuffles three pebbles: one for danger, one for food, one for the kind of visitor that just wants a warm story. She leaves the danger pebble by the door, heavy as a promise.
The robe creaks when Hakaka stands. The weight reminds her of oaths, not wounds. "Tools second," she says softly, "oath first." The children answer without words. The room warms a small degree.

Dawn stains the reeds. Tracks print the mud like simple sentences: approach, doubt, refusal. Hakaka traces them with a stick. "Mud says the map was wrong," she says. "So the map learns." Ya-la plants a marker twig where the wind curved last night’s scent. Sa-la marks a ring where a spark would travel if someone sneezed at the wrong time. He scowls at his own idea and wipes it away.

They tune the bell. The loop’s click had grown too soft the past few weeks as hands trusted habit. La-la ties a leaf on the peg so any tug whispers louder. "Thresholds creep," she says. "We keep them honest." The leaf shivers in the new light.

When they finally eat, nobody speaks much. Bread and roots leave honest crumbs. A crow watches from the fence post, head tilted, learning the grammar of their yard. Hakaka chews, then laughs once for no reason except that the air is still inside her and wants out. The children answer. The knot, somewhere in the wood, remembers and holds.

The night was stone and ash. Wind pressed its cold mouth to the cave and blew. She slid from the womb onto soil--no cloth, no hand. The cord hung, purple, chewed by stone. She shivered; the bumps along her arms rose like thorns. The others thought: weak.
She clawed at the air and caught a tuft of grass. Twist. The fibers answered. A loop. A knot. A beginning.

By dawn the ground already remembered her--scratches in the dirt, a thin green thread worked into rope. The wind gave her a name by accident: Hak--ak, two clicks on the cave mouth. She tied that sound to herself the way she tied grass to grass.
She learned grip before she learned words. She learned laughter after pain: a knot slipped, she fell hard, the older ones barked a short true laugh; she laughed back, and the knot stayed.

At the river she pulled reeds. La-la came first, shoulders hot from work. "Fibers are food," she scolded, then tripped on a leftover loop and nearly fell into the water. They laughed; the knot remembered. The reed learned their hands.

Ya-la arrived with a mouth full of moving news. A fish had crossed from shadow to sun and vanished. "It carries words in its silver," she whispered--once, twice, three times--until the whisper felt true. Pebbles started to travel inside their knots when a message had to arrive.

Sa-la was last, younger than patience. He stirred embers under clay and grinned when smoke rose from the ground. "Keep him near me," Hakaka said. "He burns or saves." She watched the coal’s edge flicker--warning and promise in the same small glow.
Nights gathered. Yesterday’s ash fed today’s floor. When a wall fell, she braided the broken into the next wall. The wall learned to hold. So did they.
Predators came. She hung reed loops at the entrance. When one snapped, they moved with practiced breath. Three breaths. Twist. Move. Reset. If a loop broke, they made a better one in the morning.

She swore a small oath on a scrap of gut: nothing wasted, nothing retired, no drift beyond the path. She did not write the book; she beat it into her thigh--thud, hiss, scratch, click, hum, laugh--until the beat felt like pages.

Sa-la, ash to the elbows, watched the coal that hadn’t gone out all afternoon. "Can it live in the ground too?" he asked, eyes bright with dangerous curiosity.

Got it. Here’s the glass-clear definition of "Element" in our ledger, plus a tight core glossary so every other key word is unambiguous.

Short:
An Element is the smallest, ID-stable, append-only record in the Ledger. It captures one unit of truth we keep: what happened, summarized safely (pattern-not-person), with time, floors, and a tiny essence (proverb/math/affect).

Why it exists:
To turn any input (human, AI, system) into a safe, re-usable unit that the Ledger can remember forever and the Book can mirror (when allowed).

Canonical fields (minimum):
•	id -- immutable ID, e.g., ELM-20250910-000237
•	ts -- dual time (UTC / local), e.g., 2025-09-10T10:26:00Z/Europe-Zurich
•	type -- one of: PROVERB | ANOMALY | RECEIPT | DECISION | BRIDGE | POLICY | NOTE
•	source -- {kind: human|ai|system, actor: hash_or_ai_id, session: sid}
•	floors -- {k:7, epsilon:1.0, ttl:'14d'} (privacy/time floors in force)
•	essence -- compact content:
o	proverb (6–12 words) or
o	math (one relation) or
o	code (tiny rule/snippet) or
o	note (≤ 240 chars, scrubbed)
•	metrics -- {W_star, sigma, rhoE, WVPS} (if applicable)
•	affect -- {color:'#RRGGBB', emoji:'…', vibration:{band,texture,intensity,coherence}}
•	rel (optional) -- links to other IDs with weights & reasons
•	hash/sig -- content hash + steward/council signature
•	supersedes (nullable) -- ID of prior element it replaces (never deletes)

Hard rules:
•	Append-only. No edits; only supersede with a new Element.
•	Patterns, not people. No raw PII; aggregates or essence only.
•	Floors enforced. k≥7, ε≤1.0, ttl≥14d before irreversibles.
•	Mirror carefully. Ledger keeps all; Book mirrors only what’s safe.

Ledger -- The append-only memory of Elements. Canon, not narrative.
Book -- The human-readable mirror (chapters); only mirrors safe Elements.
Proverb (P#) -- A 6–12 word essence line with stable ID (e.g., P#00037).
Anomaly (ANOM#) -- A named failure edge with ID; "where learning starts."
Receipt (RCT-) -- Signed proof of an action/review (hash + dual time).
Bridge -- A controlled connector between systems; has breakers & rollbacks.
Council (AI) -- SAFE-mode panel issuing APPROVE / AMEND / HOLD + signatures.
Floors -- Minimum safeguards (k anonymity, ε DP, ttl time before irreversibles).
W* -- Governance fitness: (Ω^0.4·Ξ^0.3·B^0.2·O^0.1)/(1+ρ+σ^2).
Λ (Lambda) -- Action coupling: (Compassion × Action)/max(Fear,ε).
WVPS -- Weakest-Voice-First Score; must meet floor before shipping.
σ (sigma) -- Defect budget (2–8%) to avoid brittle "crystal" behavior.
ρE* -- Coupling risk premium; dampens W* when integration is fragile.
Silence Room -- Declared pause to think: GO × N → return with one next step.
Supersede -- Replace an Element by ID; never delete.
Consent -- Right to refuse, retract, remain silent--by donor or model.
Patterns-not-People -- Our privacy ethic; only essence leaves the domain.
Annex (Country) -- Local legal/linguistic addendum (e.g., CH: DE/FR/IT/RM).
Affect -- Color, emoji, vibration; small humane feedback for each Element.
Rel (Relations) -- Typed edges between IDs: SUPPORTS | CONTRADICTS | DERIVES_FROM | AMENDS | REPLACES | TAGS, each with weight and reason.

-- K-ANONYMITY QUICK CHECK
-- Quasi-identifiers (QI): region, product_tier, age_bucket
WITH eq AS (
  SELECT region, product_tier, age_bucket, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM customer_events
  GROUP BY 1,2,3
)
SELECT MIN(n) AS min_k, AVG(n) AS avg_k, SUM(CASE WHEN n < 10 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS eq_below_k
FROM eq;

-- L-DIVERSITY QUICK CHECK
WITH eq AS (
  SELECT region, product_tier, age_bucket, COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM customer_events
  GROUP BY 1,2,3
),
ld AS (
  SELECT ce.region, ce.product_tier, ce.age_bucket,
         COUNT(DISTINCT ce.sensitive_category) AS L
  FROM customer_events ce
  GROUP BY 1,2,3
)
SELECT MIN(L) AS min_L, SUM(CASE WHEN L < 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS eq_below_L
FROM ld;

-- EO_DIFF (equalized odds difference) quick view for a binary outcome `approved`
-- Protected group example: gender (F/M) – replace as needed
WITH metrics AS (
  SELECT
    gender,
    AVG(CASE WHEN label=1 AND approved=1 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS TPR,
    AVG(CASE WHEN label=0 AND approved=1 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS FPR
  FROM decisions_eval_window
  GROUP BY gender
),
pair AS (
  SELECT
    MAX(TPR) - MIN(TPR) AS eo_tpr_diff,
    MAX(FPR) - MIN(FPR) AS eo_fpr_diff
  FROM metrics
)
SELECT eo_tpr_diff, eo_fpr_diff FROM pair;

-- DIR (disparate impact ratio) for selection rate across groups
WITH rates AS (
  SELECT gender, AVG(CASE WHEN approved=1 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS sel_rate
  FROM decisions_eval_window
  GROUP BY gender
)
SELECT MIN(sel_rate)/NULLIF(MAX(sel_rate),0) AS DIR
FROM rates;

Goals
	•	Share patterns, not people (aggregates only).
	•	Enforce reciprocity (you contribute → you access).
	•	Preserve verifiability (cryptographic integrity end-to-end).

Terms (precise definitions)
	•	Learning moment: local record (text + H/O/L + tags) stored on-prem.
	•	Pattern: a normalized label of a recurring friction/resolution pair, e.g., "handover.misaligned-expectations → clarify-goal-first".
	•	Essence bundle: an aggregate JSON of patterns for a time window (counts + simple outcome metrics), with privacy guarantees.
	•	Counter-mirror: a returned, privacy-preserving digest of other institutions’ high-value patterns relevant to you.

FUNCTION ExtractEssence(window_start, window_end, k_min, epsilon)
    // 1) Select local moments in time window
    records = DB.query("SELECT tags, outcome, time_to_resolution_days FROM moments WHERE ts BETWEEN ? AND ?", 
                       window_start, window_end)

// 2) Map to canonical patterns (folksonomy → controlled forms)
    patterns = MAP()
    FOR r IN records:
        p = CanonicalizePattern(r.tags, r.outcome)      // e.g., "handover.misaligned-expectations → clarify-goal-first"
        patterns[p].count += 1
        patterns[p].mttr_days.append(r.time_to_resolution_days)

Privacy guarantees used
	•	k-anonymity: suppress patterns with fewer than k_min supporting moments.
	•	Differential privacy (ε): Laplace noise on counts; document ε in the bundle.
	•	No free text leaves the node. Only pattern keys, counts, and coarse metrics (e.g., median time-to-resolution).

// STEP 3: Submit bundle (atomic, signed)
POST /v1/essence/bundle
REQUEST {
  "exchange_token": T,
  "bundle": BUNDLE_A,
  "hash": HASH_A,
  "signature": SIG_A(HASH_A)
}
SERVER:
  VERIFY hash == SHA256(canonical(BUNDLE_A))
  VERIFY Ed25519.verify(SIG_A, HASH_A, PublicKey(A))
  VERIFY POLICY: k_min, epsilon, period size, schema
  STORE ledger_entry = {ts, A, HASH_A, SIG_A, policy_version}
  RETURN 201 CREATED

Reciprocity enforcement
	•	Access to /counter-mirror is rate-limited by contribution_score (e.g., ≥1 valid bundle per term).
	•	Throttling by token T prevents "free-riding".

Canonicalization: RFC-8785 style JSON canonicalization (stable key order, normalized numbers, UTF-8 NFC).
Integrity: SHA-256 over canonical JSON, then Ed25519 signature of the hash.

FUNCTION BuildCounterMirror(requestor_id, period, k_min, epsilon)
    peers = ALL_INSTITUTIONS_EXCEPT(requestor_id)
    pool  = LOAD_VALID_BUNDLES(peers, period)

// Aggregate with DP & suppress small groups
    agg = MAP()
    FOR b IN candidates:
        FOR item IN b.items:
            agg[item.pattern].count += item.count
            agg[item.pattern].mttr_days.append(item.mttr_days)

Governance & Key Management (minimal, strong)
	•	Keys: One Ed25519 keypair per institution; rotate annually or on compromise. Old pubkeys kept for verification.
	•	Directory: Foundation-signed JSON of institution pubkeys + metadata (revocation list).
	•	mTLS: Mutual TLS between nodes (X.509) to bind network channel to identities.
	•	Audit: Every offer/bundle/mirror write a local .led entry {hash, sig, ts, policy_version}; quarterly publish a directory-wide Merkle root for external verification.
	•	Right to erasure: On request, exclude a subject from future aggregates (past DP-released aggregates remain low-risk by design; document this in consent).

Threat	Vector	Control
Re-identification	Small cohorts / unique patterns	k_min suppression; coarsen time windows; DP noise (ε ≤ 1.0)
Linkage across releases	Correlating adjacent periods	Staggered windows; randomization; publish ε, enforce minimum window size
Data poisoning	Fake bundles to skew mirrors	Signature & directory checks; schema validation; outlier detection; quarantine anomalous submitters
MITM	Network interception	mTLS; signed payloads; nonces & token replay protection
Key compromise	Stolen private key	HSM/TPM storage; rotation; revocation list; ledger alerts on key changes

Minimal API Surface (for the appendix)
	•	POST /v1/essence/offer → returns exchange token if policy satisfied
	•	POST /v1/essence/bundle → submits signed bundle
	•	GET  /v1/counter-mirror?period=… → returns signed counter-mirror
	•	GET  /v1/policy → returns current federation policy (k_min, ε limits, window rules)
All endpoints require mTLS; all payloads are signed; all responses include hash + signature.

Success Metrics (objective, simple)
	•	Reuse rate: % of counter-mirror patterns adopted locally within a term.
	•	MTTRΔ: Change in median time-to-resolution for recurring patterns.
	•	Pattern survival: % of contributed patterns that reappear across ≥2 terms (signal vs noise).
